301.10000000000002Substation Procedural Review - Part 1: PM, Briefs, SOPs, & SMPsCourse Title:301.1 Substation Procedural Review - Part 1: PM, Briefs, SOPs, & SMPs
Course Structure:Module 1: Preventative Maintenance Guide
• Utilizing the Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard
Module 2: Job Briefings
• Adhering to job briefing guidance for processes and procedures.
• Referencing WAC 296-45-135
Module 3: Standard Operating Procedures
• Locating and describing when to use specific SOPs relating to substations and procedures
Module 4: Standard Maintenance Procedures (SMPs)
• Locating and describing when to use specific SMPs relating to substations and procedures
Course Duration:3 Hours0 Minutes3
Activity-Based Learning:3 Hours0 Minutes3
Course Description:This course guides participants through practical exercises using the Traction Power Substation Preventative Maintenance Guide and current procedural standards. Learners will complete hands‑on tasks including conducting job briefings aligned with WAC 296-45-135, locating and applying active asset IDs to correctly identify equipment, and identifying when to use specific Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Standard Maintenance Procedures (SMPs) for substation tasks. Through scenario‑based workshops and guided walkthroughs, participants will practice documenting maintenance actions, verifying procedural compliance, and troubleshooting common procedural gaps to reinforce safe, consistent substation work practices.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Use the Traction Power Substation Preventative Maintenance Guide to identify and list three routine preventive tasks for a specified substation asset. • Perform a guided walkthrough of the maintenance standard to locate the correct inspection interval and acceptance criteria for a given component. • Conduct a mock job briefing for a sample maintenance task, verbally communicating hazards, controls, required PPE, and individual roles in accordance with WAC 296-45-135. • Complete a job-briefing checklist from a provided scenario and submit the documented briefing for instructor review. • Locate and record the active asset ID for a named substation component using the asset ID list. • Prepare a documented maintenance task plan that includes the asset ID, task description, required steps, and estimated downtime. • Document completion of a prescribed set of maintenance steps (photos/notes) and demonstrate how to verify task closure per procedure. • Locate and cite the appropriate Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for a presented operational scenario and outline the step-by-step actions required. • Select and apply the correct Standard Maintenance Procedure (SMP) for a given maintenance task and demonstrate the critical checkpoints to verify completion. • Compare two near-miss scenarios and identify where procedural adherence failed; draft corrective actions and documentation required to address each failure. • Execute a short tabletop troubleshooting exercise to resolve a procedural ambiguity, documenting the chosen procedure and justification for use. • Participate in a peer review of a completed procedure, providing actionable feedback on compliance, documentation quality, and safety considerations.

301.10000000000002Substation Procedural Review - Part 2: Work OrdersCourse Title:301.1 Substation Procedural Review - Part 2: Work Orders
Course Structure:Module 1: Work Orders
• Exploring Substation Work Order in EAMS
• Finding and Using active asset IDs for Substation Work Order entries into EAMS
Course Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Activity-Based Learning:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Course Description:This course teaches technicians how to use AssetWorks for accurate, compliant maintenance documentation through hands‑on practice and demonstrations. Participants will log in, navigate environments and location selection, search and verify assets, and create repair orders while avoiding common errors (e.g., selecting "NEW PM"). The module covers selecting correct repair reason and task IDs, writing complete 3C notes with tech IDs, recording parts and time (direct/indirect), and attaching required documents. Learners will review relevant WACs and PM rules (scheduling, tolerances, restrictions), distinguish finish vs. close actions, handle contractor/special project and service request workflows, and use in‑system help resources. A short training film and reference cards reinforce proper procedures, and new employees are encouraged to schedule follow‑up training with their lead.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Explain AssetWorks purpose and demonstrate how it supports maintenance management. • Log in to AssetWorks and configure basic account settings. • Select the correct site/location and demonstrate switching between Production, Test, and Test‑to‑Train environments for safe experimentation. • Search for an asset, verify its ID and nameplate data, and confirm the correct asset is selected for work. • Create a repair order from a selected asset and show how to avoid selecting "NEW PM" (explain consequences). • Choose the appropriate Repair Reason ID for a given fault scenario using the provided ID card. • Assign a Task ID to a repair activity and demonstrate when to use the General Task ID. • Compose complete 3C notes for a sample job, include tech IDs (not radio IDs), and remove editorial/sensitive information. • Add parts to a repair record and indicate alternative sourcing (e.g., shop stock) when parts are not ordered from MSC. • Watch and discuss the training film emphasizing accurate WO entry and high‑quality notes. • Record direct and indirect time on a sample WO, categorize entries correctly, and add required comments. • Identify applicable WACs for WPS tasks from the reference card and apply the general WAC to a sample scenario. • Demonstrate the difference between finishing and closing a WO and finish only a WO you personally worked on (reference Admin SMP 25.20). • Explain PM creation, compare PM Scheduled Date vs Due Date, apply tolerance rules, and identify risks of finishing a PM early. • Differentiate Contractor and Special Project WOs and assign appropriate attributes per the summary card. • Describe the Service Request workflow, create a sample SR, and show chief review points before conversion to a WO. • Attach and complete common WO associated documents (photos, permits, test records) to a sample order. • Navigate and use in‑system help screens to locate guidance and troubleshooting tips. • Apply PM work restrictions by identifying non‑permitted repair actions on PM WOs and noting allowable consumables. • Schedule follow‑up training with a lead and outline topics for additional hands‑on practice.

301.2Substation Right-of-Way Walk-Trough InspectionCourse Title:301.2 Substation Right-of-Way Walk-Through Inspection
Course Structure:Module 1: Switchgear Component and Equipment Review
• Hands‑on review of common substation switchgear components, their function, and inspection/maintenance checkpoints.
Module 2: R2G System Review
• R2G Walkthrough Visual Inspection Baseline: SoundTransit Eastlink Secheron Cubicle
• R2G Walkthrough Visual Inspection Comparison: Siemens Manufacturer
Module 3: Transfer Trip Review
• Locate transfer trip hardware in the field and substation, understand protection logic, and practice finding/isolating transfer trip circuits.
Module 4: Visual Inspections
• How to Perform Visual Inspections of the Following
o LCMS Central Panel
o Grounding
o Battery Chargers
o DC Control Voltage
o Batteries
o HVAC
o Network Equipment
o Emergency Trip
o Fire Alarm Panel
o Smoke Detectors
o Fire Extinguishers
o Eye Wash
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Activity-Based Learning:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This course is a Right-of-Way Walk‑Through Inspection learning event that is activity‑based, and combines hands‑on equipment review, cubicle comparisons, transfer‑trip locating, and comprehensive visual inspection practice to prepare technicians for field inspections. Through guided walk‑throughs and simulated exercises, participants will identify and assess switchgear components, compare R2G cubicle layouts (Secheron vs Siemens), locate and trace transfer‑trip hardware and protection logic in the field, and execute full substation and ROW inspections—covering LCMS panels, grounding, batteries/chargers, HVAC, fire and safety systems, network equipment, and site access/vegetation issues. Learners will document findings with photos and site maps, generate realistic EAMS work orders with asset IDs, and produce corrective action recommendations to ensure compliance, safety, and maintainability.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Identify and tag five major switchgear components on a training unit (bus, breaker, CT/VT, isolator, control cubicle). • Demonstrate a visual check for loose connections, corrosion, oil leaks, and arc evidence on a breaker assembly. • Measure and record nameplate ratings and verify they match one provided equipment spec sheet. • Submit a practical checklist with instructor verification of one corrected deficiency. • Complete a side‑by‑side visual inspection of a Secheron cubicle and a Siemens cubicle, recording three differences in layout, labeling, or access. • Trace and document the R2G signal path from primary equipment to relay/cubicle, identifying test points and protective relays. • Execute a simulated component replacement procedure: isolate, tag, swap a non‑energized module, and update the equipment log. • Take part in two station rotations (Secheron and Siemens), R2G signal tracing worksheet, hands‑on module swap exercise with instructor sign‑off. • Physically locate the transfer trip components in a mock substation layout (rear cabinet, DC/AC mains, protection cubicle) and mark their positions on a site map. • Explain and diagram the transfer trip sequence for a breaker trip event and identify where a field crew would verify status. • Perform a simulated breaker‑trip verification including checking equipment door protection (33) and documenting required actions. • Engage in a site map marking exercise where you group tabletop sequencing of a transfer trip event, hands‑on verification drill with simulated indicators. • ROW Visual Inspection of Annunciator Panel: Perform a hands‑on check of the annunciator panel, identify any active or latched alarms, acknowledge/reset where permitted, and document alarm messages, lamp failures, or wiring concerns with photos and timestamps. • ROW Visual Inspection of Grounding: Visually inspect grounding conductors, clamps, and ground rods for corrosion, loose connections, or damage; measure continuity/ground resistance at one test point and record results on the inspection checklist. • ROW Visual Inspection of Battery Chargers: Examine charger indicators, wiring, and enclosure condition; verify charger status LEDs/readouts, log output current/voltage readings, and note any abnormal temperatures, odors, or alarm conditions. • ROW Visual Inspection of DC Control Voltage: Measure and record DC control voltage at the designated test point, confirm readings are within acceptable range, and tag and create a work order for any out‑of‑tolerance values. • ROW Visual Inspection of Batteries: Conduct a visual battery inspection (terminals, case condition, electrolyte level where applicable), take specific gravity or voltage readings as applicable, photograph defects, and recommend immediate actions for identified issues. • ROW Visual Inspection of HVAC: Inspect HVAC unit operation and filters, verify temperature control in the substation space, note evidence of moisture or condensation, and document maintenance needs or service tag requirements. • ROW Visual Inspection of Network Equipment: Verify network equipment is powered, check status indicators and cabling for secure routing, record device IDs and firmware/status discrepancies, and capture screenshots or photos of any communication faults. • ROW Visual Inspection of Emergency Trip: Locate emergency trip switches and circuitry, perform a functional visual check of actuators and trip indicators (without operating live trips), and document accessibility, signage, and any protective interlock concerns. • ROW Visual Inspection of Fire Alarm Panel: Inspect the fire alarm control panel for normal status, power/fault indicators, and recent event history; record panel faults or supervisory conditions and initiate required notifications/work orders. • ROW Visual Inspection of Smoke Detectors: Visually inspect detector housings and mounting, ensure detectors are unobstructed and have current service tags/batteries, and document any missing or inoperative detectors for replacement. • ROW Visual Inspection of Fire Extinguishers: Check extinguisher presence, pressure gauge status, inspection tags, and physical condition; record missing/expired/low‑pressure units and create corrective action entries. • ROW Visual Inspection of Eye Wash: Inspect eyewash station accessibility, signage, and physical condition; verify activation/test flow (as allowed by site procedure), note obstructions or contamination, and document the need for servicing or replacement.

301.3SectionalizingCourse Title:301.2 Sectionalizing
Course Structure:Module 1: PPE – Arc Flash Distance Boundaries
• Arc‑flash calorie ratings and distance boundaries
• Required PPE and maintaining safe standoff distances
Module 2: Breaker racking procedures – Positions
• Hands‑on racking exercises on a de‑energized breaker
• Verify and document
Module 3: Tie Breakers
• Trace AC and DC tie‑breaker locations on drawings and in the field, confirm control/local/remote statuses, and simulate safe operation sequences for tie‑breaker manipulation
Module 4: Switching, Tagging, Return to Service
• How to perform complete switching, tagging, return to service sequence
Module 5: Bypass and Disconnect Operation
• Locate and operate bypass and disconnect devices on de‑energized equipment, confirm protective interlocks and control circuit status, and restore normal configuration
Module 6: Grounding OCS
• How to apply and remove temporary grounds using approved grounding sets, test continuity and bonding, and document grounding points and test results
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Activity-Based Learning:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This course is a hands‑on course that teaches technicians to read substation drawings and safely identify, operate, and verify sectionalizing equipment. Through practical exercises participants will apply arc flash PPE and establish distance boundaries, perform breaker racking and verify positions, locate and trace AC/DC tie breakers, execute switching and clearing under proper procedures, operate bypasses and disconnects, and install/remove temporary grounding per OCS procedures. Emphasis is on practicing manufacturer procedures, completing required documentation, and demonstrating end‑to‑end sectionalizing sequences so learners leave with verified competency to perform these tasks safely and in compliance with site standards.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task job briefing that documents objectives, hazards, emergency actions, communications, required permits, and PPE levels. • Identify posted arc flash calorie ratings and establish/mark corresponding distance boundaries; don and demonstrate correct PPE selection and removal. • Read and interpret substation drawings to locate sections, equipment, and tie points; verify mapping by marking drawings and photographing three field reference points. • Demonstrate breaker racking in, test, and racking out positions on a de‑energized breaker per manufacturer procedure, completing the racking checklist. • Trace AC and DC tie‑breaker circuits from drawings to field equipment, verify local/remote/control status, and document tie‑breaker locations on a circuit diagram. • Perform a complete switching → tagging → return‑to‑service sequence: execute planned switching steps, apply tags and verification checks, and restore • equipment to service per procedure while recording actions. • Locate and operate bypass and disconnect devices on de‑energized equipment, verify protective interlocks and control circuit status, and restore normal configuration per procedure. • Apply and remove temporary grounding sets to isolated conductors following OCS grounding procedures; test continuity, verify bonds, and record readings/photos. • Execute an end‑to‑end sectionalizing scenario (drawing verification → switching → racking/bypass → grounding → return to service) while narrating each safety and procedural step. • Complete required field documentation for each task (marked drawings, switching/tags records, racking and grounding checklists, operation logs) and submit for instructor review. • Identify and correct common procedural errors during live drills and justify corrective actions based on safety and manufacturer guidance. • Achieve instructor sign‑off by meeting performance criteria: accurate drawing mapping, correct PPE/boundary compliance, and safe, documented completion of racking, switching/tagging, bypass/disconnect, and grounding with no critical safety omissions.

301.39999999999998Using Specialized Traction Power ToolsCourse Title:301.4 Using Specialized Traction Power Tools
Course Structure:Module 1: Hot Stick
• Purpose and function of a Hot Stick
• Simulation: Testing via Hot Stick
Module 2: Meters and Cables
• DC Voltmeter
• Digital Voltmeter
• Grounding Cables
Module 3: Hi-Pot Testing
• Purpose and function of Hi-Pot Testing
• Simulation: Hi-Pot Testing
Module 4: Megger
• Purpose and function of a Megger
• Simulation: Testing via Megger
Module 5: IR Scan
• Purpose and function of IR Scan
• Simulation: IR Scan
Module 6: Hydraulic Crimper
• Purpose and function of Hydraulic Crimper
• Simulation: Crimping Feeders / Returns
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Activity-Based Learning:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This hands‑on REW course trains technicians to safely use specialized traction‑power tools through practical, scenario‑based exercises. Participants will learn hot‑stick operation and safe testing techniques, proper use of DC and digital voltmeters and grounding cables, and perform simulated hi‑pot and megger insulation tests; they will also conduct infrared (IR) scans to identify thermal issues and practice hydraulic crimper procedures for feeder/return terminations. Emphasis is on PPE and safe work practices, correct test setup and interpretation, tool care, and documenting results so learners leave able to confidently perform common diagnostic, test, and crimping tasks in traction power environments.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task briefing that documents objectives, hazards, required PPE, and safe work distances for all tool exercises. • Demonstrate correct selection, inspection, and safe handling of a hot stick; perform a simulated live testing exercise using hot‑stick techniques and record results. • Use DC and digital voltmeters to measure control and battery voltages and verify proper meter setup, lead connections, ranges, and safe measurement practices. • Inspect, identify, and properly deploy grounding cables; demonstrate correct connection sequence and verify continuity/bonding with a meter. • Set up and perform a simulated hi‑pot test per procedure: prepare the unit under test, connect leads and safety interlocks, run the test, interpret results, and document findings. • Configure and operate a megger (insulation resistance tester) for a simulated insulation test, interpret megger readings against acceptance criteria, and log test data. • Conduct an infrared (IR) scan simulation: identify targets, capture thermal images, interpret anomalies, and produce a brief IR report with recommended actions. • Inspect and safely operate a hydraulic crimper; perform hands‑on crimping of sample feeder/return terminations, verify mechanical/visual quality, and test continuity/resistance of crimps. • Demonstrate proper tool care, storage, and pre/post‑use inspection checklists for each specialized tool used. • Complete standardized test/report forms for each module (hot stick, meters, hi‑pot, megger, IR, crimper) and submit for instructor review. • Troubleshoot one simulated test anomaly (meter reading, hi‑pot/megger failure, IR hotspot, or poor crimp) and document corrective actions taken. • Achieve instructor sign‑off by safely performing each module exercise, correctly interpreting test results, and producing complete documentation with no critical safety omissions.

301.5Breaker Testing, Inspection, and Maintenance Course Title:301.5 Breaker Testing, Inspection, and Maintenance
Course Structure:Module 1: AC Breakers
• Inspection
• Testing
• Maintenance
Module 2: DC Breakers
• Inspection
• Testing
• Maintenance
Course Duration:12 Hours0 Minutes12
Activity-Based Learning:12 Hours0 Minutes12
Course Description:This is a 12‑hour, hands‑on REW course that trains learners on how to inspect, test, and maintain AC and DC breakers using manufacturer O&M manuals and diagrams. Through guided demonstrations and practical exercises across multiple breaker manufacturers, participants will perform visual inspections, diagnostic tests (megger, vacuum bottle checks, insulation and continuity measurements), and routine maintenance tasks while learning how to interpret manufacturer procedures and schematics to diagnose faults. Emphasis is on safe field techniques, correct test setup and result interpretation, applying manufacturer‑specific maintenance steps, documenting findings, and demonstrating competency in identifying failures and prescribing corrective actions.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task briefing covering objectives, hazards, required PPE, isolation, and emergency procedures. • Locate and reference manufacturer O&M manuals and diagrams for the specific AC and DC breaker models used in the exercises. • Perform a visual inspection of an AC breaker: identify wear, corrosion, vacuum bottle condition, contact erosion, seals, and nameplate data; document defects with photos. • Conduct insulation testing (megger) and interpret results against manufacturer acceptance criteria for an AC breaker; record test values and identify failures. • Perform vacuum bottle checks (visual and functional tests) on AC breakers per manufacturer steps and document findings. • Execute operation checks on AC breakers (open/close timing, travel, interlocks) and log timing/position data. • Complete basic maintenance tasks on an AC breaker per O&M guidance (cleaning, lubrication points, minor adjustments) and demonstrate safe reassembly. • Repeat the inspection, megger testing, vacuum bottle checks, mechanical checks, and maintenance tasks for a DC breaker, using the applicable manufacturer manuals and acceptance criteria. • Use DC and digital voltmeters, continuity testers, and appropriate test leads/cables to verify control circuits, trip coils, and auxiliary wiring on both AC and DC breakers. • Diagnose a simulated fault condition on an AC or DC breaker using test data and manuals, propose corrective actions, and document the troubleshooting steps taken. • Apply proper switching / tagging / isolation procedures for all hands‑on tests, verify zero energy where required, and demonstrate safe test setup and tool grounding where applicable. • Complete ST/KCM required (or otherwise standardized) test reports and maintenance logs for each breaker examined, including annotated drawings/diagrams, photos, measured values, and recommended next steps. • Review differences between manufacturers (controls, racking, maintenance intervals) and explain how those differences change inspection and testing workflows. • Demonstrate proper care, calibration checks, and storage of test equipment (megger, meters, vacuum test tools) and complete a pre/post‑use inspection checklist. • Achieve instructor sign‑off by meeting performance criteria: accurate documentation, correct test procedures, safe tool use, and ability to identify failures and required maintenance actions.

301.60000000000002Transformer and Rectifier Course Title:301.6 Transformer and Rectifier
Course Structure:Module 1: Transformer
• Troubleshooting
• Testing
• Maintenance
Module 2: Rectifier
• Troubleshooting
• Testing
• Diode Replacement
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Activity-Based Learning:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This course trains Rail Electrical Workers to troubleshoot, test, and maintain power transformers and rectifier systems using AVO and manufacturer guidance and field diagnostics. Through instructor‑led demonstrations and practical exercises, participants will perform visual and electrical tests on transformers (insulation, turns ratio, oil/thermal checks where applicable), execute rectifier testing and diode replacement procedures, diagnose common failure modes, apply safe isolation and grounding practices, and complete required documentation of findings and corrective actions. Emphasis is on safe tool use, accurate test setup and interpretation, component‑level repair steps, and verifying return‑to‑service readiness.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task briefing documenting objectives, hazards, required PPE, isolation, and emergency procedures. • Locate and reference manufacturer O&M and AVO Substation Maintenance test procedures for the specific transformer and rectifier units used in exercises. • Perform a systematic visual inspection of a transformer: check bushings, connections, cooling, signs of overheating, oil leaks (if applicable), and nameplate data; document defects with photos. • Conduct transformer electrical tests (insulation resistance/megger, turns‑ratio, and winding continuity) using AVO guidance, record measurements, and compare to acceptance criteria. • Interpret thermal/IR indications and oil/temperature data (where applicable) to identify developing faults or loading issues. • Troubleshoot simulated transformer faults using schematic/diagram tracing, measured test results, and stepwise diagnostic logic to isolate probable causes. • Perform routine transformer maintenance tasks per manufacturer guidance (tightening, cleaning, lubrication points) and demonstrate safe reassembly. • Establish safe isolation, verify zero energy, and apply temporary grounds where required before any hands‑on rectifier or transformer work. • Inspect and test rectifier assemblies: measure DC output, diode conduction, filter components, and control circuits using meters and test equipment. • Demonstrate diode removal and replacement on a rectifier module: safe handling, correct polarity installation, torque/fastening, and post‑replacement verification tests. • Complete fault diagnosis on a simulated rectifier failure, document troubleshooting steps, corrective actions taken, and validation test results. • Fill out standardized test and maintenance reports for transformer and rectifier work, including annotated measurements, photos, recommended actions, and return‑to‑service confirmation.

301.7Troubleshooting Course Title:301.7 Troubleshooting
Course Structure:Module 1: Review Drawings
• Review drawings for Control Power, Lockout Relay, Control Switch, PLC, Protective Relay, and Breakers
Module 2: Simulations / Activities
• Troubleshooting / Testing Scenario-Based Activities in Simulated Environment
Course Duration:16 Hours0 Minutes16
Activity-Based Learning:16 Hours0 Minutes16
Course Description:This course trains Rail Electrical Workers to troubleshoot, test, and maintain power transformers and rectifier systems using AVO Learning Guidance in Substation Maintenance I and II, along with manufacturer guidance and field diagnostics. Through instructor‑led demonstrations and practical exercises, participants will perform visual and electrical tests on transformers (insulation, turns ratio, oil/thermal checks where applicable), execute rectifier testing and diode replacement procedures, diagnose common failure modes, apply safe isolation and grounding practices, and complete required documentation of findings and corrective actions. Emphasis is on safe tool use, accurate test setup and interpretation, component‑level repair steps, and verifying return‑to‑service readiness.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Conduct a pre‑task briefing that documents objectives, hazards, PPE, isolation, and communication plans before entering the simulated or offline substation environment. • Locate and correctly identify control power, lockout relay, control switch, PLC I/O, protective relay, breaker, and transformer symbols on single‑line and control drawings. • Trace and annotate a complete control/power path (source -> control devices -> PLC/relay -> breaker/transformer) on provided drawings, marking key test points and isolation points. • Cross‑reference annotated drawings to a mockup or offline panel, physically locate at least three components, and verify labels, wiring routes, and test points. • Develop a short diagnostic plan from the drawings for an assigned circuit, specifying test steps, instruments (DMM, megger, continuity tester, IR camera, signal injector), and expected results. • Select, inspect, and safely set up test equipment (including verifying calibration tags, inspecting leads/probes, and performing zero/verification checks) before use on any circuit. • Execute safe test connections and measurements on AC and DC control circuits (voltage, continuity, insulation resistance, simulated I/O) following the diagnostic plan and site procedures. • Rotate through AC and DC mockup stations (control power, lockout relay, PLC, protective relay, breaker interface, transformer interface) and complete a station checklist of normal readings and configurations. • Apply a structured troubleshooting flow (visual -> power -> control logic -> PLC/relay -> breaker/transformer) to isolate faults on mockups and record findings on a diagnostic worksheet. • Where necessary, perform simulated switching -> tagging -> return‑to‑service sequences on offline equipment, including applying/removing temporary grounds and documenting steps on a switching/tagging form. • Enter troubleshooting scenarios where three faults are specified within a mockup or offline substation panel; use drawings and measured tests to identify all three faults within the allotted time to complete - Instructor discretion. • For each identified fault, document fault location, supporting test values, root‑cause explanation, proposed corrective action, and a verification test plan with annotated drawings and photos. • Rotate roles as troubleshooter, observer, and scribe; observers capture test techniques and provide structured feedback during scenario debriefs. • Compile and submit a complete troubleshooting package (forms, drawings, photos, and test records) for instructor scoring, then participate in a group debrief to review approaches, missed cues, and lessons learned.

301.8Cable Testing, Splicing, and TerminationsCourse Title:301.8 Cable Splicing, Testing, and Terminations
Course Structure:Module 1: Cable Splicing, Testing, Negative Return (Terminations)
• Review Cable Manufacturers' Information on Splicing Procedures
• Testing Feeder Cables
• Testing Negative Return Cables
Course Duration:6 Hours0 Minutes6
Activity-Based Learning:6 Hours0 Minutes6
Course Description:This course teaches Rail Electrical Workers safe, non‑destructive cable splicing, testing, and termination practices using manufacturer methods and field test equipment. Learners will complete a pre‑task briefing and PPE/tool checks, review splice specifications and acceptance criteria, and perform mock splices with proper conductor prep, crimping, sealing, and visual quality checks. The course covers non‑destructive pre/post‑splice inspections, insulation resistance (megger), continuity and low‑resistance testing for feeder and negative‑return cables, sheath/bonding checks, and fault‑location principles, along with troubleshooting common anomalies (poor crimps, moisture ingress, high‑resistance joints). Participants will document results with photos and standardized test reports and receive instructor review and sign‑off.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task briefing covering objectives, hazards, required PPE, isolation (no live systems), and tool checks. • Review manufacturer splice methods and specifications; identify correct materials, heat shrink/sleeves, and manufacturer acceptance criteria for common splice types. • Perform a mock splice on practice cable assemblies following manufacturer steps, demonstrating proper conductor preparation, crimping, sealing, and visual quality checks. • Demonstrate non‑destructive pre‑splice and post‑splice inspections (visual, dimensional, and continuity checks) and document splice completion with photos and a splice log. • Explain generic cable test types and limitations for in‑service cables, and justify why destructive tests are not performed on installed feeders/returns. • Set up and perform insulation resistance (megger) and continuity tests on feeder cable mockups; record test values and interpret results against pass/fail criteria. • Conduct sheath/continuity and bonding checks and simulate fault location techniques (capacitance/TDG overview) using appropriate test equipment without energizing systems. • Test negative return cable assemblies with insulation, continuity, and low‑resistance measurements; identify indications of degradation or high resistance joints. • Troubleshoot common test anomalies (poor crimp, moisture ingress, high resistance joint) using measured data and visual inspection, and propose corrective actions. • Complete standardized test reports for feeder and negative return cable tests, including measured values, photos, recommendations, and sign‑off for instructor review.

302.10000000000002Overhead Contact System Procedural Review - Part 1: PM, Brief, SOPs, & SMPsCourse Title:302.1 Overhead Contact System Procedural Review - Part 1: PM, Brief, SOPs, & SMPs
Course Structure:Module 1: Preventative Maintenance Guide
• Utilizing the Overhead Contact System Maintenance Standard
Module 2: Job Briefings
• Adhering to job briefing guidance for processes and procedures.
• Referencing applicable WACs: WAC 296-45-385, 325, 345, 375, 455
Module 3: Standard Operating Procedures
• Locating and describing when to use specific SOPs relating to substations and procedures
Module 4: Standard Maintenance Procedures (SMPs)
• Locating and describing when to use specific SMPs relating to substations and procedures
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Activity-Based Learning:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Course Description:This course guides Rail Electrical Workers through practical exercises using the Overhead Contact System Maintenance Standard and current procedural guidance. Learners will complete hands‑on tasks including conducting compliant job briefings, locating and applying asset identification for OCS components, and identifying when to use specific Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Standard Maintenance Procedures (SMPs) for overhead contact work. Through scenario-based learning and guided walkthroughs, participants will practice documenting inspection and maintenance actions, verifying procedural compliance, and troubleshooting common procedural gaps to reinforce safe, consistent OCS work practices.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Use the OCS Maintenance Standard to identify and list three routine preventive tasks for a specified OCS asset (span wire, messenger, contact wire, insulator). • Perform a guided walkthrough of the OCS maintenance standard to locate the correct inspection interval and acceptance criteria for a given component. • Conduct a mock job briefing for an OCS task that clearly communicates hazards, controls, required PPE, exclusion zones, and individual roles. • Complete a job‑briefing checklist from a provided OCS scenario and submit the documented briefing for instructor review. • Locate and record the active asset ID for a named OCS component using the asset registry. • Prepare a documented maintenance task plan that includes the asset ID, task description, required steps, safety controls, and estimated outage/track protection needs. • Document completion of a prescribed set of OCS maintenance steps (photos/notes) and demonstrate how to verify task closure per procedure. • Locate and cite the appropriate SOP for a presented OCS operational scenario (e.g., de‑energized span work, tensioning) and outline the step‑by‑step actions required. • Select and apply the correct SMP for a given OCS maintenance task (e.g., splice, tension adjustment) and demonstrate critical checkpoints to verify completion. • Compare two near‑miss scenarios involving OCS work, identify where procedural adherence failed, and draft corrective actions and required documentation. • Execute a short tabletop troubleshooting exercise to resolve a procedural ambiguity related to OCS (e.g., conflict between SOP and site constraint), documenting the chosen procedure and justification. • Participate in a peer review of a completed OCS procedure, providing actionable feedback on compliance, documentation quality, safety controls, and any suggested improvements.

302.10000000000002Overhead Contact System Procedural Review - Part 2: OCS Work OrdersCourse Title:302.1 Overhead Contact System Procedural Review - Part 2: OCS Work Orders
Course Structure:Module 1: Work Orders
• Exploring OCS Work Order in EAMS
• Finding and Using active asset IDs for OCS Work Order entries into EAMS
Course Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Activity-Based Learning:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Course Description:This course teaches technicians how to use AssetWorks for accurate, compliant maintenance documentation through hands‑on practice and demonstrations. Participants will log in, navigate environments and location selection, search and verify assets, and create repair orders while avoiding common errors (e.g., selecting "NEW PM"). The module covers selecting correct repair reason and task IDs, writing complete 3C notes with tech IDs, recording parts and time (direct/indirect), and attaching required documents. Learners will review relevant WACs and PM rules (scheduling, tolerances, restrictions), distinguish finish vs. close actions, handle contractor/special project and service request workflows, and use in‑system help resources. A short training film and reference cards reinforce proper procedures, and new employees are encouraged to schedule follow‑up training with their lead.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Explain AssetWorks purpose and demonstrate how it supports maintenance management. • Log in to AssetWorks and configure basic account settings. • Select the correct site/location and demonstrate switching between Production, Test, and Test‑to‑Train environments for safe experimentation. • Search for an asset, verify its ID and nameplate data, and confirm the correct asset is selected for work. • Create a repair order from a selected asset and show how to avoid selecting "NEW PM" (explain consequences). • Choose the appropriate Repair Reason ID for a given fault scenario using the provided ID card. • Assign a Task ID to a repair activity and demonstrate when to use the General Task ID. • Compose complete 3C notes for a sample job, include tech IDs (not radio IDs), and remove editorial/sensitive information. • Add parts to a repair record and indicate alternative sourcing (e.g., shop stock) when parts are not ordered from MSC. • Watch and discuss the training film emphasizing accurate WO entry and high‑quality notes. • Record direct and indirect time on a sample WO, categorize entries correctly, and add required comments. • Identify applicable WACs for WPS tasks from the reference card and apply the general WAC to a sample scenario. • Demonstrate the difference between finishing and closing a WO and finish only a WO you personally worked on (reference Admin SMP 25.20). • Explain PM creation, compare PM Scheduled Date vs Due Date, apply tolerance rules, and identify risks of finishing a PM early. • Differentiate Contractor and Special Project WOs and assign appropriate attributes per the summary card. • Describe the Service Request workflow, create a sample SR, and show chief review points before conversion to a WO. • Attach and complete common WO associated documents (photos, permits, test records) to a sample order. • Navigate and use in‑system help screens to locate guidance and troubleshooting tips. • Apply PM work restrictions by identifying non‑permitted repair actions on PM WOs and noting allowable consumables. • Schedule follow‑up training with a lead and outline topics for additional hands‑on practice.

302.2Catenary Walking InspectionCourse Title:302.2 Catenary Walking Inspection
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Catenary System Components
• Review and Identify Overhead Catenary System Components
Module 2: Overhead Catenary Drawings with Field Conditions
• Review and Overhead Catenary Drawings with Corresponding Field Conditions
Module 3: Overhead Catenary System Walking Inspection
• Overhead Catenary System Typical Walking Inspection
• Overhead Catenary System Impedance Bond Inspection
• Overhead Catenary System Poles, Foundation, and Grounds Inspection
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Activity-Based Learning:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This course trains Rail Electrical Workers to perform thorough walking inspections of overhead catenary systems by combining classroom review of components and drawings with field verification of real conditions. Learners will identify and inspect catenary components (contact wire, messenger, insulators, clamps, impedance bonds, poles and foundations), correlate drawings to observed field conditions, and conduct timed walking inspections that include impedance bond checks and pole/foundation/ground assessments. Emphasis is on safe work practices and clear documentation — participants will mark assets, capture photos/GPS locations, record defects against acceptance criteria, and prepare actionable inspection reports and recommended corrective actions.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task briefing documenting objectives, hazards, PPE, exclusion zones, and communications before field work. • Identify and name major OCS components (contact wire, messenger, droppers, insulators, clamps, cantilevers, impedance bonds, tension assemblies) on equipment and drawings. • Demonstrate correct visual inspection techniques for contact and messenger wires (wear, abrasion, stagger, height) and record findings. • Inspect insulators, clamps, droppers and hardware for corrosion, looseness, deformation, and secure fastening; document defects with photos. • Read and interpret catenary drawings and correlate at least three drawing elements to their exact field locations; annotate discrepancies. • Perform a timed walking inspection over a defined route, logging asset IDs/GPS, photos, observed defects, and immediate safety concerns. • Locate and inspect impedance bonds: visually assess condition, verify markings, and perform basic continuity/low‑ohm checks as permitted by procedure. • Assess poles, foundations, and grounds for cracking, rot, anchor corrosion, drainage, and bonding; record measurements/photo evidence for defects. • Measure and record key clearances and heights (using tape or laser tool) at sample locations and compare to drawing/spec limits. • Identify signs of third‑party encroachment, vegetation interference, or vandalism affecting the OCS and recommend mitigations. • Prioritize identified defects by severity and safety risk, and draft immediate corrective action recommendations. • Complete standardized inspection forms and produce an inspection report including annotated drawings, photos/GPS points, defect descriptions, severity ratings, and recommended actions. • Demonstrate safe on‑track/near‑track behavior, use of PPE, and site controls throughout the walking inspection. • Participate in a group debrief to review findings, discuss discrepancies between drawings and field conditions, and capture lessons learned for follow‑up.

Course Structure:Module 1: Review, Identify, and Inspect
• Contact Wire
• Messenger Wire
• Hangers
• Arms
• Droppers
• Arc Horn
• Clamps
• Connectors
• Sag
• Height or Offsets
• Section Breaks
• Jumpers
• Insulators
• Tensioning System
• Bypass and Disconnects
• Lightening Arrestors
Module 2: Special or Complex Catenary Configurations
• Review, Identify, and Inspect Existing Catenary Configurations that are More Complex than Standard
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Activity-Based Learning:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This course trains Rail Electrical Workers to perform quarterly visual inspections of the Catenary Inspection & Maintenance Vehicle and associated overhead catenary components. Through guided field walk‑downs, hands‑on use of checklists, and comparison to standards, participants will review, identify, and inspect key elements such as contact and messenger wires, hangers, arms, droppers, arc horns, clamps, connectors, sag and height/offsets, section breaks, jumpers, insulators, tensioning systems, bypasses, disconnects, and lightning arrestors. Learners will practice recognizing normal versus abnormal conditions, documenting defects with photos and measurements, and updating inspection records. The course also exposes REWs to special or more complex catenary configurations, where they will identify configuration‑specific risks and adapt their visual inspection techniques accordingly, ensuring consistent, safe, and thorough quarterly inspections.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Complete a pre‑task briefing that identifies objectives, hazards, PPE, and safe work limits specific to quarterly catenary visual inspections. • On the Catenary Inspection & Maintenance Vehicle and line, point out and correctly name contact wire, messenger wire, hangers, arms, droppers, arc horns, clamps, connectors, section breaks, jumpers, insulators, tensioning systems, bypasses, disconnects, and lightning arrestors. • Use the quarterly visual inspection checklist to perform a guided walk‑down of standard catenary, recording normal versus abnormal conditions for each component type. • Visually assess contact and messenger wires for wear, damage, sag, and alignment, then document findings with measurements (height/offset where applicable) and photos. • Inspect hangers, droppers, clamps, connectors, and arms for corrosion, cracks, loose hardware, and misalignment; tag and log any defects found. • Examine section breaks, jumpers, bypasses, and disconnects for mechanical integrity and proper positioning; record any abnormal conditions on the inspection form. • Inspect insulators, tensioning systems, and lightning arrestors for contamination, leakage paths, damage, and missing parts; capture GPS/photo evidence for any concerns. • Practice using the Catenary Inspection & Maintenance Vehicle’s inspection tools (e.g., measuring devices, cameras, onboard documentation systems) to collect and store inspection data. • Review example drawings and photos of special or complex catenary configurations (e.g., crossovers, tunnels, multi‑track portals), then locate and identify these configurations in the field where available or on mockups. • Compare inspection requirements for standard vs. complex configurations and adapt the checklist to capture configuration‑specific risks and additional inspection points. • Work in pairs to classify observed defects by severity and urgency, and draft recommended corrective actions for at least three real or simulated findings. • Complete and submit a full quarterly visual inspection record for an assigned segment, including checklists, annotated photos, measurements, and prioritized defect list. • Participate in a group debrief to review sample inspection packages, discuss missed or borderline conditions, and refine individual inspection techniques based on peer and instructor feedback.

302.39999999999998Catenary Mockup - Annual Hands-On InspectionCourse Title:302.4 Catenary Mockup - Annual Hands-On Inspection
Course Structure:Module 1: Safety
• PPE
• Rigging
• Fall Protection
• Pole Top Rescue
Module 2: Tools, Tension, Components, & General Troubleshooting
• Tools
• Auto-Tension Maintenance or Adjustments (Tensorex)
• Component Replacement
• Contact Wire / Cable Repair
• Messenger Wire / Cable Repair
• Cable Replacement
• Guy Wires
• Anchors or Dead Ends
• General Troubleshooting
Course Duration:16 Hours0 Minutes16
Activity-Based Learning:16 Hours0 Minutes16
Course Description:This course gives Rail Electrical Workers intensive, hands‑on practice performing an annual inspection and basic troubleshooting on a catenary mockup. Learners begin with a safety module focused on PPE, rigging, fall protection, and pole‑top rescue drills, applying procedures in realistic scenarios before moving to field work. In the tools, tension, components, and general troubleshooting module, participants use specialized tools to perform auto‑tension checks and adjustments (e.g., Tensorex), contact and messenger wire assessments and repairs, cable replacement, guy wire inspection, and anchor/dead‑end verification. Through guided exercises, they will practice diagnosing common issues (damaged components, incorrect tension, compromised supports), performing safe corrective actions on the mockup, and documenting findings and repairs. Emphasis is on real‑world skill application: climbing and positioning, using tools at height, verifying safe system condition. This also involves producing inspection/maintenance records that support safe, reliable catenary operations.
Activity-Based Learning Objectives:
• Conduct a pre‑task safety briefing that identifies objectives, hazards, PPE requirements, fall‑protection needs, and rescue plan for catenary mockup work. • Put on, adjust, and inspect required PPE (including fall‑protection harness, lanyards, and helmets) and demonstrate proper use while climbing and working at height. • Set up, inspect, and use rigging and access equipment (ladders, platforms, climb systems) on the catenary mockup according to site procedures. • Perform a pole‑top rescue drill on the mockup, safely lowering a “downed” worker (dummy or equivalent) following the approved rescue sequence. • Identify and select the correct tools for catenary work (e.g., Tensorex/auto‑tension tools, wire grips, cutters, crimpers, torque tools) and complete a tools‑inspection checklist. • Measure and record auto‑tension system values with Tensorex (or equivalent), compare to specified targets, and perform a supervised adjustment to bring tension into tolerance. • Inspect contact and messenger wires for wear, damage, incorrect stagger/height, and hardware defects; document findings with measurements and photos. • Perform a mock contact or messenger wire repair: isolate the section, prepare the conductors, install approved connectors, and verify mechanical/electrical integrity. • Remove and replace a catenary cable on the mockup, including proper tensioning, securing hardware, and final visual/measurement checks. • Inspect guy wires and associated hardware (insulators, strain clamps, turnbuckles) for corrosion, cracks, misalignment, slack, or over‑tension; adjust or tag defects as appropriate. • Examine anchors and dead‑ends for movement, cracking, corrosion, and proper attachment; torque‑check or mark components per procedure. • Complete a general troubleshooting exercise on the mockup by locating and diagnosing a set of pre‑planted defects (e.g., damaged fittings, incorrect tension, loose hardware) using a structured inspection route. • Prioritize identified defects by severity and risk, and draft recommended corrective actions for at least three issues, including temporary mitigations if needed. • Fill out an annual hands‑on inspection form for the mockup, including tension readings, component conditions, measurements, photos, and corrective‑action notes. • Participate in a group debrief to review inspection packages, compare troubleshooting approaches, and refine personal inspection and safety practices based on peer and instructor feedback.

301.10000000000002Power Distribution Systems: Power IsolationCourse Title:301.1 Power Distribution Systems: Power Isolation - Part 1
Power Isolation - Part 1
Course Structure:Module 1: Power Isolation: Power Down for Maintenance
• Power down the distribution system for maintenance
Module 2: Rail Feeder and Return Drawings
• Read / Interpret rail feeder and return drawings
• Identify power sections in rail feeder and return drawings
Module 3: Power Isolation: Power Control Center - Isolate
• Isolate power in / from the power control center
Module 4: Insulation Inspection and Cleaning
• Inspect insulation and wash as applicable
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This advanced course equips REWs with skills to safely execute power isolation in distribution systems. Learners will power down distribution systems for maintenance, read and interpret rail feeder and return drawings, and identify power sections. The module covers isolating systems from the power control center, ensuring safe disconnection and reconnection. Participants will inspect and clean insulation, following best practices for washing and maintenance. Emphasis is placed on understanding complex drawings, applying isolation procedures accurately, and maintaining clear communication with control centers. Trainees will document all actions and verify compliance with safety standards, preparing them for challenging real-world scenarios.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will power down distribution systems following established safety protocols and accurately document all steps taken. They will read and interpret rail feeder and return drawings and identify power sections effectively. Learners will isolate systems from the power control center, ensuring proper disconnection and reconnection procedures are followed. Participants will inspect and clean insulation according to best practices, record the condition and maintenance actions taken. Additionally, they will demonstrate effective communication with control centers throughout the isolation process and verify that all actions comply with safety standards.
Learning Objectives:• Describe the step-by-step process for safely powering down distribution systems for maintenance and explain the importance of each step. • Explain how to read and interpret rail feeder and return drawings and discuss their relevance to identifying power sections. • Identify and outline processes for isolating systems from the power control center and express the implications of proper disconnection and reconnection. • Discuss best practices for inspecting and cleaning insulation, including specific cleaning techniques and materials. • Demonstrate the ability to recognize complex drawing components and express their significance in power isolation tasks. • Apply the correct isolation procedures in a mock scenario and document the actions taken in an inspection report. • Communicate effectively with control centers during isolation procedures and provide a summary of interactions for recordkeeping. • Document all actions taken during the course, ensuring they are compliant with safety standards and formatted according to site protocols. • Evaluate case studies of real-world isolation scenarios, discussing lessons learned and improvements for future practices.

Course Description:This advanced course focuses on power isolation techniques within distribution systems. Practical exercises will enable them to effectively address real-world scenarios in power distribution systems.

302.10000000000002 Substations: Circuit Prints - InterpretCourse Title:302.1 Substations: Circuit Prints - Interpret
Course Structure:Module 1: Interpret Substation Circuit Prints
• Read and interpret circuit prints to discover and repair problems
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This advanced course teaches REWs to read and interpret substation circuit prints for troubleshooting, maintenance and safe isolation. Learners review ANSI/IEEE and local drawing conventions, single‑line and wiring diagrams, relay schematics, protection and metering circuits, instrument‑transformer secondary layouts, and terminal /c connection numbering. The module covers tracing fault paths, identifying trip and interlock logic, locating isolation points on prints and mapping those to physical plant, and using prints to plan tests and safe work sequences. Emphasis is placed on verifying as‑built vs drawing discrepancies, annotating prints, documenting findings for handover, and preparing accurate escalation packages for protection and engineering teams. Practical exercises use real prints and case scenarios to build confident, mission‑critical interpretation skills.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will interpret ANSI/IEEE and local drawing conventions and read single‑line, wiring and relay schematics. They will trace fault paths and identify trip, interlock and metering circuits on prints. Learners will locate isolation points on drawings and accurately map them to physical plant. Participants will use prints to plan tests and safe work sequences. They will detect and record as‑built versus drawing discrepancies, annotate prints, and prepare clear handover and escalation packages for protection and engineering teams.
Learning Objectives:• Describe key ANSI/IEEE and local drawing conventions and identify at least ten common schematic symbols from a supplied symbol chart. • Explain single‑line diagram components and trace the power flow from source to load on a provided print. • Read a wiring diagram and list terminal/connection numbers for three specified circuits. • Interpret a relay schematic and explain trip and interlock logic for a given protection function. • Locate instrument‑transformer secondary layouts on a print and identify CT/VT secondary terminals for three devices. • Trace a fault path on a case‑study print and document the sequence of protective operations expected. • Identify isolation points on a supplied circuit print and map those points to physical plant locations in a mock layout. • Use a circuit print to plan a test sequence, listing required isolations, test points and safety checks for the task. • Compare an as‑built field photo to the drawing, note three discrepancies, and annotate the print accordingly. • Complete an annotated print with measured values and observations and submit it as a handover package. • Prepare an escalation package from a print‑based diagnosis that includes affected equipment IDs, fault path, likely causes and recommended specialist actions. • Demonstrate proficiency by successfully interpreting and annotating a real substation print during a timed practical exercise.

Course Description:This advanced course equips REWs to troubleshoot, repair and replace a wide range of substation auxiliary components beyond primary transformers and breakers. Learners study protective relays, control and auxiliary relay contacts, UPS systems and station battery banks, secondary wiring and DC/AC auxiliary supplies. The module covers diagnostic techniques for relay logic and secondary circuits, battery health assessment and charger verification, and repair or replacement procedures for relay modules and auxiliary equipment. Emphasis is placed on correct isolation, earthing and secondary circuit safety, functional testing and timing verification, and documenting test results and repairs. Practical exercises focus on real‑world fault scenarios, coordinated handovers with protection and control teams, and knowing when to escalate complex failures to specialist engineers.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will diagnose faults in protective relays, auxiliary relay contacts, UPS systems and station battery banks, and secondary wiring; perform approved repair or replacement procedures for relay modules and auxiliary equipment; assess battery health and verify charger operation; apply correct isolation, earthing and secondary‑circuit safety measures before work; execute functional and timing tests and interpret results against acceptance criteria; document test data and repair actions clearly; coordinate handovers with protection and control teams; and recognize and escalate complex failures to specialist engineers with complete technical details.
Learning Objectives:• Describe functions and common failure modes of protective relays, auxiliary relay contacts, UPS systems and station battery banks. • Explain secondary wiring and DC/AC auxiliary supply layouts and locate key circuits on provided schematics. • Perform relay logic diagnostics using secondary injection or simulated inputs and record trip/operate responses. • Execute functional and timing tests on protective relays and compare results to specified acceptance criteria. • Inspect auxiliary relay contacts and verify contact continuity and operation, logging measured values. • Assess UPS operation by measuring input/output voltages and transfer times, and document deviations from normal ranges. • Perform battery health checks (voltage, internal resistance or specific gravity where applicable) and classify condition per site criteria. • Verify battery charger output and charging profile, and record charge current and voltage trends over a defined test period. • Apply correct isolation, earthing and secondary‑circuit safety procedures on a mock task and obtain team verification. • Carry out approved repair or replacement procedures for relay modules and auxiliary components and have work verified by the instructor. • Complete standardized test reports with all measurements, observations and remedial actions, and submit for review. • Prepare and submit a detailed escalation package for complex or unsafe failures including test data, diagrams, recommended actions and contact points.

303.10000000000002Overhead Contact System Components: Troubleshooting Methods and Best Practices - Part 1 Course Title:303.1 Part 1 Overhead Contact System: Contact Wire Troubleshoot, Repair, Replace
Part 1 Overhead Contact System: Contact Wire Troubleshoot, Repair, Replace
Course Structure:Introduction and Scenario
Module 1: Safety Procedures for OCS Contact Wire Repair / Replacement
• Follow proper safety protocols for preparing to work on the OCS Contact Wire and Messenger Wire
Module 2: Overhead Contact System Tools
• Receive knowledge and gain proficiency in preparing to work on the OCS contact wire and messenger wire
Module 3: OCS: Contact Wire and Messenger Wire – Repair / Replace
• Execute the steps needed to perform contact wire and messenger wire replacement.
Course Duration:20 Hours0 Minutes20
Course Description:This advanced course prepares REWs to troubleshoot, repair and replace contact wire on the Overhead Contact System. Learners study common contact‑wire faults, wear patterns and electrical/mechanical failure modes. The module covers diagnostic techniques including visual assessment, wear measurement, continuity and tension testing, and pantograph interaction checks. Participants practice approved splice, termination and replacement methods, set tension to local parameters, and verify stagger and alignment. Emphasis is placed on correct isolation, earthing and rigging before wire work, safe lifting and team signaling during replacements, tool calibration and PPE selection. Trainees learn post‑work mechanical and electrical checks, defect classification, accurate report writing, and escalation procedures for complex or safety‑critical findings. Practical, instructor‑led exercises replicate live scenarios to build competence for field operations.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will identify common contact‑wire faults and wear patterns, perform visual, wear, continuity and tension inspections, and evaluate pantograph interaction. They will apply approved splice, termination and replacement methods, set and verify tension, stagger and alignment to local parameters, and complete post‑work mechanical and electrical checks. Learners will follow correct isolation, earthing and rigging procedures, use calibrated tools and appropriate PPE, document findings with standard reports, classify defects, and escalate complex or safety‑critical issues for specialist follow‑up.
Learning Objectives: • Describe common contact‑wire faults and wear patterns and match each to probable causes. • Explain how pantograph interaction affects contact‑wire condition and list two inspection indicators of poor interaction. • Perform a visual contact‑wire inspection using the provided checklist and record at least five condition observations. • Measure contact‑wire wear with calipers, record measurements in millimeters, and compare results to local wear limits. • Test continuity and conductor resistance with a multimeter, log readings, and classify outcomes as Good / High‑Resistance / Open. • Measure wire tension with a tension meter, record values, and state whether readings meet local parameter tolerances. • Calculate and set correct stagger for a given span from supplied data and record the computed stagger value. • Explain and demonstrate approved splice and termination techniques on the training rig and obtain instructor verification. • Replace a section of contact wire on a mock setup, set tension to specification, and verify alignment and stagger. • Apply the correct isolation, earthing and rigging sequence before wire work on a simulated task and obtain team sign‑off. • Select and confirm calibration of required tools and PPE prior to performing repairs and document tool IDs. • Conduct post‑work mechanical and electrical checks, record results on the standard form, and justify the equipment status. • Classify identified defects as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and justify each classification with measurement evidence. • Complete a standard inspection and repair report with measurements, photos, actions taken and recommended follow‑up. • Prepare and submit an escalation package for any safety‑critical or complex fault including test data, diagrams and recommended immediate actions.

Part 2 Overhead Contact System Components: Supporting Structure - Repair

Module 2: Overhead Contact System Components: Supporting Structure - Repair
• Repair supporting structure of the overhead contact system
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This advanced course prepares REWs to inspect, diagnose and repair OCS supporting structures to industry standards. Learners study bracketry, cantilevers, insulator mounts, fittings and pole integrity, and identify corrosion, fatigue, weld and fastening failures. The module covers repair techniques including secure bolting, plate repair, welding preparation, fitting replacement, foundation remediation and temporary support installation. Participants practice safe rigging, lifting and positioning methods, and follow permit, isolation and earthing requirements prior to structural work. Emphasis is placed on load calculations, torque and welding quality checks, post‑repair NDT/visual inspections, and verifying mechanical and electrical interfaces with the OCS. Trainees record repair steps, produce handover documentation, and escalate complex or safety‑critical defects to engineering specialists.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will inspect and diagnose OCS supporting‑structure defects, identify corrosion, fatigue, weld and fastening failures, and select appropriate repair methods. They will perform secure bolting, plate repairs and fitting replacements, prepare and verify welding work, and install temporary supports or foundation remediation measures. Learners will apply safe rigging, lifting and positioning techniques, complete load and torque checks, and conduct post‑repair inspections. They will verify mechanical and electrical interfaces with the OCS, document repair steps and handover details, and escalate complex or safety‑critical defects to engineering specialists.
Learning Objectives: • Describe types of OCS supporting‑structure components (brackets, cantilevers, insulator mounts, fittings) and explain typical failure modes. • Inspect a given structure and record at least five condition indicators (corrosion, fatigue, weld cracks, loose fasteners) on the provided checklist. • Diagnose supporting‑structure defects and select an appropriate repair method from the approved options, justifying the choice in writing. • Calculate safe working loads for a specified lift scenario and state required rigging components and safety factors. • Demonstrate correct rigging, lifting and positioning techniques on a training rig and have the instructor verify compliance. • Perform secure bolting or fitting replacement to torque specification and record torque values. • Prepare a plate repair or welding task, complete pre‑weld checks, and verify welding quality against acceptance criteria after instructor inspection. • Install a temporary support or carry out basic foundation remediation per procedure and document materials and steps used. • Conduct post‑repair NDT or visual inspection, record measured results, and compare to acceptance limits. • Verify mechanical and electrical interface integrity with the OCS after repair and log continuity/tension or alignment checks. • Complete a standardized repair record and handover document with measurements, materials used, and next‑step recommendations. • Prepare and submit an escalation package for complex or safety‑critical defects including photos, measurements, load calculations and recommended mitigation.

304.10000000000002Overhead Catenary Systems (OCS): Troubleshoot and RepairCourse Title:304.1 Overhead Catenary Systems (OCS): Troubleshoot and Repair: Part 1 Overhead Catenary System Messenger Contact Wire and Hangers - Repair
Part 1 Overhead Catenary System Messenger Contact Wire and Hangers - Repair
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Catenary Systems: Contact Wire - Repair
• Troubleshoot and repair contact wire
Module 2: Overhead Catenary Systems: Hangers - Adjust / Repair

Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This advanced course trains REWs to troubleshoot, repair and replace messenger and contact wire and associated hangers on the Overhead Catenary System. Learners study fault diagnostics, wear patterns and interaction effects with pantographs. The module covers detailed measurement and assessment techniques for wear, tension, stagger and alignment, plus approved splice, termination and hanger replacement methods. Participants practice rigging, lifting and safe positioning for wire and hanger work, and follow permit, isolation, grounding / earthing and verification procedures before any live task. Emphasis is placed on tool selection and calibration, correct application of tension and stagger to local parameters, inspection of fittings and hangers for corrosion or fatigue, post‑repair mechanical and electrical checks, accurate documentation of measurements and actions, and escalation of complex or safety‑critical defects to engineering specialists. Practical, instructor‑led exercises replicate field scenarios to build competence for live maintenance.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will diagnose faults and wear in messenger and contact wire systems and assess pantograph interaction effects. They will measure and record wear, tension, stagger and alignment using calibrated tools and compare results to local parameters. Learners will perform approved splices, terminations and hanger replacements, and apply correct tension and staggering to specification. They will set up rigging, lifting and work positioning following permit, isolation and earthing procedures. Participants will complete post‑repair mechanical and electrical checks, document measurements and actions accurately, and escalate complex or safety‑critical defects to engineering specialists.
Learning Objectives:• Describe common fault types and wear patterns in messenger and contact wire and explain how pantograph interaction affects wear. • Explain required tool calibration checks and confirm calibration status before taking any measurements. • Measure contact‑wire wear with calipers, record values in millimeters, and determine compliance with local wear limits. • Measure conductor tension and stagger using site tension and positioning tools, log readings, and state whether values meet specified parameters. • Inspect hangers and fittings for corrosion, fatigue or looseness, record three condition indicators, and recommend maintenance actions. • Perform an approved splice on the training rig, document technique and have the instructor verify compliance with the splice standard. • Execute a termination procedure to specification and record continuity and insulation test results. • Replace a hanger assembly on a mock setup following permit, isolation and earthing steps, and obtain team verification of completion. • Set up rigging and lifting for a wire replacement scenario, calculate safe working loads, and justify chosen rigging configuration. • Apply the correct isolation, grounding/earthing and verification sequence on a simulated task and capture verification timestamps. • Conduct post‑repair mechanical checks (alignment, tension, stagger) and electrical checks (continuity, resistance), and record all measurements on the standard form. • Classify defects found during inspection or repair as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and justify each classification with measured evidence. • Complete a standardized repair and inspection report with photos, measurements and recommended follow‑up actions. • Prepare and submit an escalation package for complex or safety‑critical findings including test data, photos, and suggested immediate mitigations.

304.10000000000002Overhead Catenary Systems (OCS): Troubleshoot and RepairCourse Title:304.1 Overhead Catenary Systems (OCS): Troubleshoot and Repair: Part 2 Overhead Catenary System - Tensioning
Part 2 Overhead Catenary System - Tensioning
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Catenary Systems: Wire Tension - Check / Adjust
• Check and adjust wire tension
• Check and adjust fixed tension wires
• Check and adjust auto (constant) tension
Course Duration:TBD HoursTBD MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This advanced course trains REWs in troubleshooting, adjusting and repairing OCS tensioning systems for safe, reliable catenary performance. Learners study manual and automatic (constant) tension mechanisms, BWA and Tensorex components, and common tension‑related failure modes and wear patterns. The module covers diagnostic techniques, tool calibration, tension measurement methods, and procedures for re‑tensioning conductors to local parameters. Participants practice isolation, earthing and rigging required before tension work, safe greasing and servicing of auto‑tension wheels, and calculation of target tensions for varying spans and temperatures. Emphasis is placed on verifying post‑work settings, documenting measurements and maintenance actions, and escalating complex or unsafe conditions to specialist engineers.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will explain manual and auto tensioning mechanisms and identify common tension‑related faults. They will perform calibrated tension measurements and calculate target tensions for specified spans and temperatures. Learners will execute re‑tensioning procedures for BWA and Tensorex systems and grease/service auto‑tension wheels per procedure. They will apply correct isolation, earthing and rigging before tension work and verify post‑work settings against acceptance criteria. Participants will document measurements and maintenance actions accurately and escalate complex or unsafe conditions to specialist engineers with required technical details.
Learning Objectives:• Describe manual and automatic (constant) tensioning mechanisms and list three common tension‑related failure modes. • Explain BWA and Tensorex component functions and identify four wear indicators on inspection photos. • Verify calibration of a tension meter and record calibration ID and date before measurement. • Measure conductor tension on a training span, record the reading in specified units, and compare it to the target value. • Calculate target tension for a given span and temperature using the local formula and show all working steps. • Perform a re‑tensioning procedure on a mock setup to achieve the calculated target and record final readings. • Grease and service an auto‑tension wheel per procedure, log lubricant type and quantity, and mark application points. • Apply correct isolation, earthing and rigging sequences on a simulated task and obtain team verification/sign‑off. • Inspect post‑tension settings for alignment, stagger and tension, record three verification measurements, and judge acceptability. • Classify any out‑of‑limit or unsafe conditions as Minor / Major / Unsafe and justify the classification with measured data. • Complete the standard maintenance record with measurements, actions taken and recommended follow‑up, and submit it for review. • Prepare and submit an escalation package for complex or unsafe findings including measurements, photos and recommended immediate actions.

304.10000000000002Overhead Catenary Systems (OCS): Troubleshoot and RepairCourse Title:304.1 Overhead Catenary Systems (OCS): Troubleshoot and Repair: Part 3 Arc Horns, Support Structure, Span Wire, Down Guy, and Snow Equipment

Course Structure:Module 1: Arc Horns and Support Structure
• Check and adjust arc horns
• Check and adjust support structure

Course Duration:TBD HoursTBD MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This advanced course trains REWs to troubleshoot, repair and maintain arc horns, support structures, span wire systems, down guys and snow‑clearing equipment within the OCS. Learners study failure modes, interaction effects and acceptance criteria for each component. The module covers structured visual and mechanical inspections, alignment and clearance checks, tension and continuity testing, and approved repair techniques for brackets, span wires and guy anchors. Participants practice safe rigging, lifting and temporary support installation, and follow permit, isolation and earthing procedures before any work. The course also addresses snow‑equipment mounting, operation checks and seasonal readiness tasks. Emphasis is placed on tool calibration, post‑repair verification, NDT where applicable, accurate documentation, and escalations to engineering specialists for complex or safety‑critical defects. Practical, scenario‑based exercises replicate field conditions to build competence for live maintenance.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will inspect and diagnose arc horns, support structures, span wires, down guys and snow‑clearing equipment against acceptance criteria; perform tension and continuity tests and record measured values; execute approved repair techniques for brackets, span wires and guy anchors and verify results with post‑repair checks; apply correct isolation, earthing and permit procedures and demonstrate safe rigging, lifting and temporary support installation; carry out snow‑equipment mounting and operational readiness checks; use calibrated tools and perform NDT where required; document inspections, tests and repairs in standard reports; and prepare and submit escalation packages for complex or safety‑critical defects to engineering specialists.
Learning Objectives:• Describe functions and common failure modes of arc horns, support structures, span wires, down guys and snow‑clearing equipment. • Explain acceptance criteria for each component and identify three measurable indicators used in inspections. • Perform a structured visual and mechanical inspection on a sample component and record at least five condition observations using the provided checklist. • Measure span‑wire and down‑guy tension with calibrated tools, record readings in N or kgf, and compare values to acceptance limits. • Test continuity of span and feeder conductors, log resistance readings in ohms, and classify results as Good / High‑Resistance / Open. • Conduct alignment and clearance checks for arc horns and document measured gaps against clearance standards. • Demonstrate approved repair techniques for bracket, span‑wire and guy‑anchor faults and have the instructor verify completion to standard. • Install a temporary support and demonstrate correct lifting/rigging configuration for a specified load, showing calculated safe working load. • Perform NDT (visual or specified method) on a repaired weld or fitting, record findings, and compare to acceptance criteria. • Mount and verify operation of a snow‑clearing device per procedure and log functional test results. • Apply correct permit, isolation and earthing sequences on a mock task and obtain team verification/sign‑off. • Verify calibration of measurement tools before use and record tool ID and calibration date on the test sheet. • Complete a standardized inspection and repair report with photos, measurements and recommended actions, and submit an escalation package for any safety‑critical defects.
